items.label: text
items.text: In most of the simple examples you will meet at International GCSE, each atom in a covalent bond supplies one electron to the shared pair of electrons. That doesn't have to be the case. Both electrons may come from the same atom.

items.label: text
items.text: Remember that, although the electrons are drawn as dots or as crosses, there is absolutely no difference between them in reality; the dots and the crosses simply show that the electrons have come from two different atoms.

items.label: text
items.text: If atoms have 8 electrons in their outer shell they have the same number of electrons as a noble gas atom – they are isoelectronic with a noble gas atom. If atoms have 8 electrons in their outer shell they have the same number of electrons as a noble gas atom – they are isoelectronic with a noble gas atom.

items.text: COVALENT BONDING IN A HYDROGEN MOLECULE

items.label: text
items.text: Covalent bonds are often shown using dot-and-cross diagrams.

items.label: text
items.text: Both hydrogen nuclei in Figure 8.3 are strongly attracted to the shared pair of electrons.

items.text: Figure 8.3 A dot-and-cross diagram for H2

items.label: text
items.text: Hydrogen atoms form diatomic molecules with the formula H2. The atoms in an H₂ molecule are joined together by a covalent bond. The covalent bond between two hydrogen atoms is very strong.

items.label: text
items.text: Molecules contain a certain fixed number of atoms, which are joined together byt    bt s       hey contain two atoms. Other sorts of molecule may have as many as thousands of atoms joined together, for example proteins and DNA.

items.label: section_header
items.text: THE SIGNIFICANCE OF NOBLE GAS STRUCTURES IN COVALENT BONDING

items.label: text
items.text: In H2, each hydrogen atom has only one electron to share, so it can only form one covalent bond. The shared pair of electrons is in the outer shell of both, therefore each atom has the same number of electrons as a noble gas atom (helium in this case).

items.label: text
items.text: Does that mean that the hydrogen has turned into helium? No. The number of protons in the nucleus hasn't changed, it is the number of protons that defines what an atom is.

items.label: text
items.text: In virtually all of the molecules you will meet at this level, electrons will be shared so that H atoms have a total of 2 electrons in their outer shell and all other atoms will have 8 electrons in their outer shell. Some people talk about the 'octet rule', referring to this 8. Remember, we are counting shared electrons as belonging to the outer shells of both atoms.

items.label: text
items.text: When there is one atom in the middle and other atoms are joined to it (as in CH or PCl) the outer atoms will virtually always have 8 electrons in their outer shell (or 2 if they are H). In fact, it is very difficult to think of an example where the outer atoms do not have 8 electrons. There are some molecules where the central atom does not have 8 electrons in the outer shell, and we will look at a couple of examples of those later on.
